kf1.tip: Rank seismometers, GPS sensors and gas sniffers by how much you would trust each one alone to warn of an eruption, and defend each place in one line.
kf1.note: A strong answer weighs what each signal actually shows. Tremors show magma rising, but earthquakes shake the ground too. A bulge shows the chamber filling, not when it will erupt. Rising sulphur dioxide is tied directly to an eruption coming. Many put gas sniffers first for that reason. The trap is trusting any one alone. The lesson says eruptions are predicted from a combination of seismic activity, gas readings and ground deformation.

kf2.tip: Link monitoring, prediction, protection and planning as a chain for an earthquake, then name the weakest link and explain how it weakens the others.
kf2.note: Your chain should run in order. Monitoring gathers fault and groundwater data, prediction interprets it, protection strengthens buildings and planning prepares people. Most name monitoring and prediction as the weakest link for earthquakes. No method predicts the day or street, only probabilities and seconds of warning. That puts the weight on protection and planning. If you named a link without saying how it weakens the others, the answer is only half done.

cs1.tip: Sketch a timeline from the P-waves arriving to the S-waves arriving, and mark what Japan's early-warning system does in the seconds between.
cs1.note: Check your sketch against this. P-waves arrive first and are fast but harmless. Sensors detect them, calculate the size and send alerts to phones, trains and factories. In the gap, bullet trains stop, gas mains shut off and people take cover. The slower, destructive S-waves arrive last. Label the gap as seconds, with ten seconds as enough to act. A strong sketch notes that this saved hundreds of lives in the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake.
